title: Social clubs, Creole audiences and black audiences
summary: Creole social-club crowds dance from the first note while other black crowds wait until half drunk.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I noticed a bit over, in fact, since I've known you, that you don't do a lot of club days.

No. And you know, there really ain't no money. I don't know if you do anything. You work like him. Right. But you don't make no money. And I've just gotten out of that. I play. You see these people call me. I play with these people. I play for the Autocrat Circle. And from the time the band start, see, okay, I'll say this. See, there are Creole people downtown. It's more like white people. And I say like this. See, the reason we like playing for white people, people like me, is from the time the music start until it's in, they're dancing.

This is the way the Creoles are. From the time the band starts telling, they're dancing. But you see them other black people, you know what they're doing. Sitting out looking at them. They ain't going to move until they get half drunk. And then when they get half drunk, then they want to start playing. And they can sit there an hour and a half getting drunk. And then when two o'clock comes, it's time to go home, they just begin to start playing another
So there's a social difference. And then when you're playing, you know, you're playing a lot of people, you know, and I'll...
